clue.text: Clumsy person barging into girl all over the place

indicators.note: one piece barging into another forces its way inside it

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
a lob is an old word for a lout or clumsy oaf

explanation.surface: An awkward oaf crashes into a young woman and sends things flying everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worldwide is found everywhere, which is the sense of the idiom about scattering widely.

clue.text: OT character in the Bible — Saul?

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows, across the word break

explanation.surface: A quiz question: is Saul an Old Testament figure in the Bible?
explanation.walkthrough: OT is the Old Testament; the brother of Jacob is in the end of Bible and start of Saul.
explanation.definitionFit: The hairy elder twin of Jacob appears in Genesis, a book of the Old Testament.

clue.text: Assigned a time and attempted to get round objection

indicators.note: the attempt word is to wrap itself around the objection word

parts.note: attempted means tried
a but is an objection, as in 'no ifs or buts'

explanation.surface: Someone was given a time slot and tried to wriggle past a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: To credit or ascribe something to a person is to assign it to them.

clue.text: Fellow's arresting a group of criminals for court appearances

indicators.note: to arrest is to hold, so the fellow's word holds the next pieces inside it

parts.note: a fellow is a he, and he's is the contraction of 'he is'
a ring is a gang of criminals, such as a drugs ring

explanation.surface: A man is busy nicking a criminal gang, leading to appearances in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Trials and sessions in which a judge listens to a case are the occasions people appear in court.

clue.text: Is suspicious? Alarm less activated with time

indicators.note: activated suggests the letters are set in motion and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone grows suspicious after a timed alarm becomes less sensitive.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to sense that something underhand is going on, to have one's suspicions.

clue.text: Blemishes and dreadful harm inflicted on one yellow flower

parts.note: mars, as a verb, means spoils or blemishes

indicators.note: dreadful suggests the word harm is badly mangled

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
gold is a yellow colour

explanation.surface: Spots and terrible damage have been inflicted on a single yellow bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a wetland plant with bright golden blooms, also called kingcup, so an example of a bloom.

clue.text: Salesman's fetishes — disposing of book for shilling — leading to debt collector's interventions

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative; the possessive adds no letter

indicators.note: disposing of one letter in favour of another means swapping them, with 'for' saying which comes in

parts.note: fetishes are obsessions
S is the abbreviation for the old British shilling coin

explanation.surface: A salesman's strange fixations end up bringing in the bailiffs.
explanation.walkthrough: In OBSESSIONS the B (book) is replaced by S (shilling), giving OSSESSIONS; the shilling was a pre-1971 British coin.
explanation.definitionFit: When a lender takes back goods after unpaid debts, those seizures are what a bailiff carries out.

clue.text: Frontless lingerie item — it'll have you whirling

indicators.note: frontless means the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: a teddy is a one-piece undergarment for women

explanation.surface: A lingerie piece cut low at the front is enough to make your head spin.
explanation.definitionFit: A swirling current of water or air spins whatever is caught in it round and round.

clue.text: Expose doped steed without ulterior motive

parts.note: to disinter is to dig up and expose

indicators.note: a doped horse is not itself, so its letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Reveal the racehorse that was drugged, with no hidden agenda.
explanation.definitionFit: An impartial person has no personal stake, so they act with no hidden motive.

clue.text: Doll Tearsheet, say, Shakespeare presented in another way

indicators.note: presenting the word the other way round means reading its letters backwards

parts.note: Shakespeare is known as the Bard

explanation.surface: A theatre programme note on how Shakespeare's Doll Tearsheet might be staged differently.
explanation.walkthrough: Doll Tearsheet is a prostitute in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 2; the old word for such a woman is a slatternly drab.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic term for a harlot or slattern, which fits the Shakespearean character as an example.

clue.text: Posh meal, not initially about to become dull

indicators.note: the first letter of the meal word is dropped

parts.note: supper is an evening meal
C stands for circa, Latin for about
to rust is to become dull and corroded

explanation.surface: An upmarket dinner that, without fresh beginnings, is turning stale.
explanation.definitionFit: The aristocracy or upper classes are known by this phrase, so it means upper-class, smart.

clue.text: Charles keeps parasites in cups

indicators.note: keeps means holds within, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: lice are parasitic insects

explanation.surface: A man named Charles keeps bugs in his drinking vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: Goblets used for wine, especially at Communion, are a kind of drinking vessel.

clue.text: Yachtsman formerly from coastal city

definitions.meaning: Sir Francis of that name was a pioneering round-the-world solo sailor of the 1960s
a cathedral city in West Sussex near the south coast of England

explanation.surface: A former sailor hails from a seaside city.
explanation.definitionFit: The sailor's surname and the English cathedral city near the Channel coast share one name.

clue.text: Cheap wine? Note empties in irritation

indicators.note: the emptied word sits inside the irritation word

parts.note: a bind is a nuisance or irritation

indicators.note: empties means the inside letters are cleared out, leaving only the outer two

explanation.surface: Annoyance at a bottle of plonk, noted as finished.
explanation.walkthrough: N and E, the outsides of Note, go inside BIND. A bin end is the last bottles of a wine sold off cheaply.
explanation.definitionFit: Leftover bottles from a merchant's stock are sold at a discount, so cheap wine by example.

clue.text: Odd square attic with limited edition interior — it's not for everyone

indicators.note: interior says one piece is placed within the other
odd suggests the letters are out of their normal order

parts.note: ED is a shortened, limited form of the word edition

explanation.surface: A strange square loft, fitted out with a limited-edition interior, will not suit all tastes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' scrambles the eleven letters of square attic, giving ACQUIRTASTE, and 'limited' tells you edition is cut to its usual short form.
explanation.definitionFit: Something one learns to like only through exposure is not to the liking of all people.

clue.text: Fruit tree cut down, computer system dismissing one arrangement of five

indicators.note: cut down means the word is shortened by its final letter

parts.note: the quince is a tree bearing hard yellow fruit

indicators.note: dismissing means a letter is sent away from the word

parts.note: Unix is a computer operating system
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A fruit tree is felled while a computer setup gets rid of something.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the pattern of five dots on dice, four at the corners and one in the centre.

clue.text: Angle brackets in the last elaboration

indicators.note: to bracket is to enclose, so the angle word encloses the next word

parts.note: to angle is to fish with a rod and line

explanation.surface: A note on typesetting: angle brackets go in the final round of polishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angle brackets' looks like the typographic symbol; Angle is FISH and brackets is the containment.
explanation.definitionFit: A final coat or polish on a piece of work is its last refinement.

clue.text: Dodge that is observed in autumn month?

indicators.note: the phrase is seen inside the month, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: Sep is an abbreviation for September, an autumn month
id est is the Latin for 'that is', usually shortened to i.e.

explanation.surface: An evasion of the kind that turns up in September.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that is' is not a link phrase here: it is the Latin id est, written out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: To step to one side avoids a blow or an issue, which is to evade it.

clue.text: Source of tourists engaging in emotional responses?

definitions.text: Source of tourists engaging in emotional responses?

indicators.note: engaging means taking in and holding, so the responses word holds the letter

parts.note: sighs are emotional responses, such as of longing or relief

indicators.note: the source of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Something that makes tourists sigh with feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: T, the start of tourists, goes inside SIGHS; the whole clue describes what draws gasps from visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: Famous attractions draw visitors and stir them to emotion, so they are a source of tourism.

clue.text: Theatrical jester's acknowledgement of a hit about Society fashion

indicators.note: about means placed around, so the fencing word goes round the rest

parts.note: touché is what a fencer says to admit being hit
ton is an old word for fashion or high style

explanation.surface: A stage clown admits being scored against regarding a fashionable social set.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'theatrical jester' is the court fool in Shakespeare's As You Like It; 'ton' is an old borrowing from French for high fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: The court fool in Shakespeare's As You Like It bears this name, an example of a stage jester.

clue.text: Illness not beginning at all

indicators.note: not beginning means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a fever is an illness

explanation.surface: A disease that never really starts.
explanation.definitionFit: In phrases like 'did you ever', the word means at any time, so in any way at all.

clue.text: Follower of rock subculture landed husband

parts.note: to land something is to get it, so landed means got

explanation.surface: A rock fan with a dark style has secured a husband.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the gloomy, black-clad rock music scene that arose in the 1980s.

clue.text: Legendary leader virtuous in discounting success

indicators.note: discounting means leaving the following piece out

parts.note: virtuous means good
a go can mean a success, as in 'make a go of it'

explanation.surface: A mythical chief is good-hearted but plays down his achievements.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief god of Norse mythology heads the pantheon, a ruler from legend.

clue.text: Church festival I started unexpectedly in middle of week

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go in between the middle pair
the middle of a four-letter word is its central two letters
unexpectedly suggests the letters land in a surprising order

explanation.surface: Someone began a religious celebration on a sudden whim in midweek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpectedly' scrambles I started into ASTERTID; the middle of a four-letter word is its central pair, which goes either side.
explanation.definitionFit: The season following the Christian resurrection feast is a period of church celebration.
